metadata.name: math-mcp
metadata.description: Foundation MCP server providing symbolic algebra (SymPy) and GPU-accelerated numerical computing (NumPy/CuPy). Serves as computational primitive layer for Quantum, Molecular, and Neural MCPs.

architecture.pattern_explanation: Hub-and-Spoke: Info tool serves as discovery hub. Tools are grouped by domain (symbolic, numerical, transforms, optimization). Resource Provider: Exposes computed arrays and constants as MCP resources for cross-MCP workflows.

tool_relationships.info_tool: Hub - provides progressive discovery of all capabilities
tool_relationships.numerical_group: Array creation and manipulation, feeds into linalg/fft tools
tool_relationships.transform_group: Consumes arrays from numerical tools, produces transformed arrays
tool_relationships.optimization_group: Consumes functions (as strings) or arrays, produces optimal solutions

array_id.purpose: Reference large arrays (>10MB) stored in /tmp/mcp-array-cache/ without serializing to JSON

expression_id.purpose: Reference complex symbolic expressions without re-parsing

gpu_strategy.fallback: Graceful degradation to NumPy if CuPy unavailable
gpu_strategy.memory_management: Shared memory pool (80% of GPU memory), configured in config.kdl
gpu_strategy.array_interface: Unified via compute_core.arrays.get_array_module() - returns cupy or numpy

resource_architecture.constants: Read-only math constants (pi, e, golden_ratio) at constants://math/{name}
resource_architecture.arrays: Computed arrays at array://{array_id} - returns serialized format based on size
resource_architecture.expressions: Symbolic expressions at expr://{expression_id} - returns SymPy LaTeX or string

enforced_questions.question: How should we handle arbitrary precision vs standard precision?
enforced_questions.recommendation: Default to float64, provide optional 'precision' parameter for mpmath arbitrary precision
enforced_questions.rationale: Most workflows need speed (float64 on GPU). Arbitrary precision is opt-in for specialized cases.

enforced_questions.question: Should symbolic tools execute arbitrary Python code?
enforced_questions.recommendation: NO - only parse SymPy expressions, validate against safe symbol set
enforced_questions.rationale: Security: Prevent code injection. Use sympy.sympify() with evaluate=False, validate symbols.

enforced_questions.question: What are size limits for arrays?
enforced_questions.recommendation: Default max 100M elements (configurable in config.kdl), fail fast with clear error
enforced_questions.rationale: Prevent OOM errors. 100M float64 = 800MB, reasonable for 8GB GPU.

enforced_questions.question: Should we cache expensive computations?
enforced_questions.recommendation: YES for symbolic simplification (memoize), NO for numerical (state changes)
enforced_questions.rationale: Symbolic operations are pure functions. Numerical operations may have side effects (GPU state).

enforced_questions.question: How to handle numerical instability warnings?
enforced_questions.recommendation: Return warnings in response metadata, don't fail unless NaN/Inf produced
enforced_questions.rationale: Ill-conditioned matrices common in real workflows. User should see warnings but get results.

tools.name: symbolic_solve
tools.description: Solve symbolic equations or systems of equations using SymPy. Supports algebraic equations, transcendental equations, and systems.

equations.description: Equation(s) to solve. Use '=' for equations, or expression (assumed = 0). Examples: 'x**2 - 4', 'x**2 + y**2 = 25'

variables.description: Variable(s) to solve for. Auto-detected if not provided.

output_schema.solutions: array<object> - Each solution as {variable: value} dict
output_schema.expression_id: string - URI for reusing solution expressions
output_schema.warnings: array<string> - Any warnings (multiple solutions, infinite solutions, etc.)

tools.relationships: Standalone. Solutions can feed into symbolic_simplify or symbolic_diff via expression_id.
use_cases: Solve systems of linear equations for circuit analysis
user_stories: As a student, I want to solve homework equations and see step-by-step work
As an engineer, I want to solve circuit equations symbolically
As a researcher, I want to find analytical solutions to differential equations

implementation_guide.usage_patterns: Parse equations with sympify, create symbols, call solve, format results
implementation_guide.pseudocode: vars = symbols(variables); eqs = [sympify(eq) for eq in equations]; sols = solve(eqs, vars, domain=domain); return {solutions: sols, latex: latex(sols), expression_id: store(sols)}

error_handling.parse_error: Return clear error with suggested fix

implementation_guide.security: CRITICAL: Use sympify(evaluate=False) to prevent code execution. Validate symbols are alphanumeric.

tools.performance: fast (~10-100ms for simple equations, ~1s for complex systems)

tools.name: symbolic_diff
tools.description: Compute symbolic derivatives of mathematical expressions. Supports partial derivatives, multiple variables, and arbitrary order.

expression.description: Expression to differentiate. String or expression_id from previous tool

variable.description: Variable to differentiate with respect to

order.description: Derivative order (1 for first derivative, 2 for second, etc.)

tools.relationships: Can consume expression_id from symbolic_solve or symbolic_integrate. Produces expression_id for further operations.
use_cases: Find velocity from position function (first derivative)
user_stories: As a physicist, I want to derive equations of motion from potential energy
As a student, I want to check my calculus homework
As a data scientist, I want symbolic gradients for custom loss functions

implementation_guide.usage_patterns: Retrieve or parse expression, call diff, simplify, store result
implementation_guide.pseudocode: expr = get_expression(expression); var = symbols(variable); deriv = diff(expr, var, order); if simplify: deriv = simplify(deriv); return {derivative: str(deriv), expression_id: store(deriv), latex: latex(deriv)}
implementation_guide.optimization: Cache simplified expressions to avoid re-simplification

tools.name: symbolic_integrate
tools.description: Compute symbolic integrals (indefinite or definite) using SymPy. Supports single and multiple integrals.

limits.description: Integration limits [lower, upper] for definite integral. Use strings for symbolic limits.

output_schema.numerical_value: number or null - Numerical value for definite integrals (if computable)
output_schema.is_convergent: boolean or null - For improper integrals, whether they converge

tools.relationships: Standalone or consumes expression_id from other symbolic tools.
user_stories: As a student, I want to compute integrals for calculus homework
As an engineer, I want to find area moments of inertia symbolically
As a physicist, I want to evaluate path integrals

required_functions: sympy.oo - infinity symbol for improper integrals
implementation_guide.usage_patterns: Parse expression, create integral with limits if provided, evaluate, simplify
implementation_guide.pseudocode: expr = get_expression(expression); var = symbols(variable); if limits: result = integrate(expr, (var, limits[0], limits[1])); else: result = integrate(expr, var); numerical = result.evalf() if result.is_number else null; return {integral: str(result), expression_id: store(result), numerical_value: numerical}

error_handling.non_integrable: Return error with explanation (e.g., 'integral does not converge')
error_handling.timeout: If integration takes >30s, return timeout error

tools.performance: fast to moderate (~10ms-1s depending on complexity)

tools.name: symbolic_simplify
tools.description: Simplify symbolic expressions using SymPy's simplification algorithms. Supports various simplification strategies.

output_schema.expression_id: string - URI for reusing simplified expression
output_schema.reduction_ratio: number - Ratio of simplified/original expression lengths (indication of simplification effectiveness)

tools.relationships: Post-processor for other symbolic tools. Consumes expression_id from symbolic_solve, symbolic_diff, symbolic_integrate.
user_stories: As a student, I want to simplify messy algebra results
As a mathematician, I want to verify trigonometric identities

implementation_guide.usage_patterns: Retrieve expression, apply strategy, compare lengths, return result
implementation_guide.pseudocode: expr = get_expression(expression); original_len = len(str(expr)); simplified = apply_strategy(expr, strategy); simplified_len = len(str(simplified)); return {simplified: str(simplified), expression_id: store(simplified), reduction_ratio: simplified_len/original_len}
implementation_guide.caching: Memoize simplification results for identical expressions

tools.name: create_array
tools.description: Create numerical arrays with various initialization patterns. GPU-accelerated when available.

shape.description: Array dimensions [rows] or [rows, cols] or [depth, rows, cols]

function.description: Function string for 'function' fill_type. Variables: x, y, z (0-indexed coordinates). Examples: 'x**2', 'sin(x)*cos(y)', 'x**2 + y**2'

linspace_params.description: Parameters for linspace: start and stop values

output_schema.data: array or null - Inline data for small arrays (<10MB)

tools.relationships: Foundation tool for numerical workflows. Produces arrays consumed by matrix_multiply, fft, solve_linear_system.
use_cases: Create zero-initialized array for simulation state
Create coordinate grids for wave simulations
Initialize potential energy arrays for quantum mechanics
user_stories: As a researcher, I want to create a Gaussian potential for quantum simulations
As a data scientist, I want to generate random test data on GPU
As a physicist, I want to create coordinate meshgrids for field simulations

required_functions: xp = gpu_manager.get_array_module() - get cupy or numpy
xp.linspace(start, stop, num) - evenly spaced values
xp.arange(start, stop, step) - range of values
evaluate_function(function_str, shape) - parse and evaluate function over grid
implementation_guide.usage_patterns: Determine backend (GPU/CPU), create array with appropriate method, serialize based on size
implementation_guide.pseudocode: xp = get_array_module(use_gpu); if fill_type == 'zeros': arr = xp.zeros(shape, dtype); elif fill_type == 'function': arr = evaluate_function(function, shape); size_mb = arr.nbytes / 1e6; if size_mb > 10: return {array_id: store(arr), uri: f'array://{array_id}', size_mb: size_mb}; else: return {data: arr.tolist(), shape: shape, backend: backend}
implementation_guide.function_evaluation: For 'function' fill_type: create meshgrid, parse function safely with sympify, evaluate using lambdify
implementation_guide.size_limits: Enforce max size from config (default 100M elements). Fail fast with clear error if exceeded.
implementation_guide.serialization: Small arrays (<10MB): inline JSON. Large arrays: write to /tmp/mcp-array-cache/{array_id}.npy, return URI

tools.performance: fast (<100ms for million elements on GPU)

tools.name: matrix_multiply
tools.description: Multiply two matrices using GPU-accelerated matrix multiplication (cuBLAS via CuPy). Optimized for large matrices.

output_schema.result: array<array<number>> or null - Inline result for small matrices
output_schema.array_id: string or null - URI for large result matrices

tools.relationships: Consumes arrays from create_array or other numerical tools. Produces arrays for further operations.
user_stories: As a graphics programmer, I want to multiply transformation matrices
As a data scientist, I want fast matrix multiplication for large datasets
As a physicist, I want to apply Hamiltonian operators to quantum states

required_functions: xp.matmul(a, b) - matrix multiplication (cuBLAS on GPU)
gpu_manager.synchronize() - ensure GPU operations complete before timing
implementation_guide.usage_patterns: Load or parse input matrices, verify shapes compatible, perform matmul, serialize result based on size
implementation_guide.pseudocode: xp = get_array_module(use_gpu); A = load_array(a); B = load_array(b); if A.shape[1] != B.shape[0]: raise ValueError('incompatible shapes'); start = time(); C = xp.matmul(A, B); gpu_manager.synchronize(); elapsed = time() - start; return serialize_result(C, elapsed)

error_handling.shape_mismatch: Return clear error: 'Matrix A has shape (M, K), B has shape (L, N), but K must equal L'
error_handling.out_of_memory: Fall back to CPU if GPU OOM, add warning to response

implementation_guide.performance_optimization: Use xp.matmul which dispatches to cuBLAS (GPU) or OpenBLAS (CPU) - highly optimized

tools.performance: very fast (~1ms for 1000x1000 on GPU, ~100ms on CPU)

tools.name: solve_linear_system
tools.description: Solve linear system Ax = b using LU decomposition or least squares. GPU-accelerated via cuSOLVER.

method.description: Solution method: 'auto' selects based on matrix properties

output_schema.condition_number: number or null - Condition number (if computed)

tools.relationships: Consumes arrays from create_array or matrix operations. Endpoint tool (no further chaining typically).
user_stories: As an engineer, I want to solve circuit equations quickly
As a scientist, I want to fit experimental data to a model
As a student, I want to verify my linear algebra homework

required_functions: xp.linalg.solve(A, b) - solve square systems (LU decomposition)
xp.linalg.lstsq(A, b) - solve overdetermined systems (QR decomposition)
xp.linalg.cholesky(A) - Cholesky for symmetric positive definite
implementation_guide.usage_patterns: Load matrices, select method based on shape/properties, solve, compute residual and warnings
implementation_guide.pseudocode: xp = get_array_module(use_gpu); A = load_array(a); b = load_array(b); if method == 'auto': method = select_method(A); if method == 'lu': x = xp.linalg.solve(A, b); elif method == 'least_squares': x, residuals = xp.linalg.lstsq(A, b); residual = xp.linalg.norm(A @ x - b); cond = xp.linalg.cond(A); warnings = check_conditioning(cond); return {solution: x.tolist(), residual: float(residual), condition_number: float(cond), warnings: warnings}

error_handling.singular_matrix: Return error: 'Matrix is singular (determinant = 0), system has no unique solution'
error_handling.ill_conditioned: Return solution with warning: 'Matrix is ill-conditioned (cond={cond}), solution may be inaccurate'

implementation_guide.warning_thresholds: Condition number >1e10: severe warning, >1e6: moderate warning

tools.name: fft
tools.description: Compute Fast Fourier Transform using GPU-accelerated cuFFT (or NumPy FFT on CPU). Supports 1D, 2D, 3D transforms.

axes.description: Axes along which to compute FFT. Null for all axes.

output_schema.result: object - FFT result with real/imag components
output_schema.array_id: string or null - URI for large results
output_schema.magnitude: array or null - Magnitude spectrum (|FFT|) for small results

tools.relationships: Pairs with ifft for round-trip transforms. Used heavily by quantum-mcp for split-step Fourier method.
user_stories: As a signal processor, I want to analyze frequency content of audio
As a physicist, I want to propagate quantum wave functions in momentum space
As an image analyst, I want to filter images in frequency domain

implementation_guide.usage_patterns: Load signal, determine dimensionality, call appropriate FFT function, serialize result
implementation_guide.pseudocode: xp = get_array_module(use_gpu); signal = load_array(signal); start = time(); if signal.ndim == 1: result = xp.fft.fft(signal, norm=norm); elif signal.ndim == 2: result = xp.fft.fft2(signal, norm=norm); else: result = xp.fft.fftn(signal, axes=axes, norm=norm); elapsed = time() - start; magnitude = xp.abs(result); return serialize_complex_result(result, magnitude, elapsed)
implementation_guide.complex_serialization: Store real and imaginary parts separately in output: {real: [...], imag: [...], magnitude: [...]}

tools.performance: very fast (~5ms for 1M points on GPU, ~50ms on CPU)

tools.name: ifft
tools.description: Compute Inverse Fast Fourier Transform. Inverse of fft tool.

spectrum.description: Frequency domain data (complex). Provide as {real: [...], imag: [...]} or array_id

axes.description: Axes along which to compute IFFT

norm.description: Normalization mode (should match fft norm for round-trip)

output_schema.result: object {real, imag} or array - Reconstructed signal
output_schema.array_id: string or null - URI for large results
output_schema.is_real: boolean - True if imaginary part is negligible (real signal)

tools.relationships: Inverse of fft. Forms round-trip with fft for Fourier-space operations.
use_cases: Reconstruct time-domain signal from frequency modifications
Quantum wave function propagation (momentum → position space)
user_stories: As an audio engineer, I want to apply frequency filters and reconstruct audio
As a physicist, I want to propagate wave functions back to position space

required_functions: xp.allclose(spectrum.imag, 0) - check if result is real
implementation_guide.usage_patterns: Load spectrum (reconstruct complex array from real/imag), call ifft, check if result is real
implementation_guide.pseudocode: xp = get_array_module(use_gpu); spectrum = reconstruct_complex(spectrum); result = xp.fft.ifftn(spectrum, axes=axes, norm=norm); is_real = xp.allclose(result.imag, 0); if is_real: return {result: result.real.tolist(), is_real: True}; else: return {result: {real: result.real.tolist(), imag: result.imag.tolist()}, is_real: False}

tools.performance: very fast (same as fft, ~5ms for 1M points on GPU)

tools.name: optimize_function
tools.description: Find minimum of a scalar function using scipy.optimize methods. Supports constraints and bounds.

function.description: Function to minimize. Use variables x, y, z. Examples: 'x**2 + y**2', '(x-1)**2 + (y-2)**2'

initial_guess.description: Initial guess for optimization [x0] or [x0, y0] or [x0, y0, z0]

bounds.description: Bounds for each variable [[x_min, x_max], [y_min, y_max], ...]. Null for unbounded.

output_schema.gradient_norm: number or null - Final gradient norm (if applicable)

tools.relationships: Standalone optimization tool. No dependencies on other tools.
user_stories: As a researcher, I want to fit model parameters to experimental data
As an engineer, I want to optimize design parameters

required_functions: scipy.optimize.minimize(objective, x0, method, bounds, tol) - main optimizer
sympy.lambdify(variables, expression) - convert string function to callable
parse_function_safely(function_str) - parse and validate function string
implementation_guide.usage_patterns: Parse function string, create callable, call scipy.optimize.minimize, return result
implementation_guide.pseudocode: vars = extract_variables(function); expr = sympify(function); objective = lambdify(vars, expr, 'numpy'); result = scipy.optimize.minimize(objective, initial_guess, method=method, bounds=bounds, tol=tolerance); return {optimal_x: result.x.tolist(), optimal_value: float(result.fun), success: result.success, iterations: result.nit, message: result.message}
implementation_guide.security: CRITICAL: Use sympify with evaluate=False, validate variables are safe. Use lambdify with 'numpy' backend only (not 'eval').

tools.performance: moderate (~100ms-10s depending on function complexity and dimensions)

tools.name: find_roots
tools.description: Find roots (zeros) of a function using scipy.optimize root-finding methods.

function.description: Function to find roots of. Use variable x. Examples: 'x**2 - 4', 'sin(x) - 0.5'

method.description: Root-finding method. 'brentq' requires bracket [a, b], others require single guess.

bracket.description: Bracket [a, b] for bracketing methods (brentq, bisect, ridder). Function must have opposite signs at a and b.

output_schema.function_values: array<number> - f(root) values (should be near zero)

tools.relationships: Numerical complement to symbolic_solve. Use when symbolic solution not possible.
use_cases: Find equilibrium points in dynamical systems
user_stories: As a mathematician, I want to find roots of transcendental equations
As an engineer, I want to solve implicit equations numerically

required_functions: scipy.optimize.brentq(f, a, b, tol) - bracketing method
implementation_guide.usage_patterns: Parse function, create callable, select appropriate method based on inputs, find root
implementation_guide.pseudocode: expr = sympify(function); f = lambdify('x', expr, 'numpy'); if method in ['brentq', 'bisect', 'ridder']: require bracket; result = scipy.optimize.brentq(f, bracket[0], bracket[1], xtol=tolerance); else: result = scipy.optimize.newton(f, initial_guess, tol=tolerance); return {roots: [result], function_values: [f(result)], converged: True}

error_handling.no_bracket: If bracketing method selected but no bracket provided, return error
error_handling.bracket_same_sign: If f(a) and f(b) have same sign, return error with suggestion to widen bracket

critical_patterns: ALWAYS accept extra parameters with warnings, never reject unless severe (security issue)
Use sparse tables in info tool for human readability, provide JSON option for automation
Progressive detail: high-confidence results get full details, low-confidence get IDs only
ID references (array_id, expression_id) save massive tokens in workflows - use aggressively
GPU manager is singleton - get instance, don't create new
Fail fast with clear errors - never return dummy data (per CLAUDE.md)
Always include backend info in responses (GPU/CPU) for transparency
Serialize large arrays to files, small arrays inline - check size threshold
security_requirements: Symbolic tools: ONLY use sympify(evaluate=False) to prevent code execution
Validate all symbolic variables are alphanumeric (no __builtins__, eval, etc.)
Lambdify: ALWAYS use 'numpy' or 'math' backend, NEVER 'python' or custom
Array size limits: enforce max from config.kdl (default 100M elements)
No arbitrary code execution - parse expressions only
Resource URIs: validate format, prevent path traversal (use UUID-based naming)
performance_optimization: Use unified array interface (compute_core.arrays) for automatic GPU/CPU dispatch
Memory pool sharing via GPUManager reduces overhead
cuBLAS/cuFFT automatically used by CuPy - no manual calls needed
Large array serialization: .npy format is 10x faster than JSON
Stream ordered memory allocator for GPU enables sharing across tools
error_handling_patterns: Numerical instability: return result with warnings, don't fail
GPU OOM: graceful fallback to CPU with warning in response
Singular matrices: clear error message explaining what's wrong
Timeout for expensive operations: symbolic integration >30s, fail with clear message
testing_strategy: Unit tests for all tools with CPU backend (pytest -m 'not gpu')
Integration tests for cross-MCP workflows (Math → Quantum)
Performance benchmarks: matrix multiply, FFT at various sizes

✓ Implement array serializer with size-based switching
✓ Wrap SymPy functions with security validation
✓ Implement info tool with progressive discovery
✓ Add resource handlers for constants, arrays, expressions

✓ Add integration tests for example workflows
✓ Create config.kdl with GPU settings and size limits
